newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Swedish Riksbank posts steady surplus for 1996.
newsitem.headline: Swedish Riksbank posts steady surplus for 1996.

text.p: Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, said on Thursday that its before balance-sheet allocations for 1996 showed a surplus of 18.6 billion crowns ($2.5 billion) against a surplus of 18.8 billion crowns in 1995.
The Riksbank's annual report, to be presented to parliament on Thursday, said 4.6 billion crowns of this would be allocated to the balancing fund against 14.3 billion crowns a year ago.
The Riksbank said it will transfer 8.1 billion crowns to the government as it did in 1995.
Foreign operations in 1996 generated a surplus of 14.2 billion crowns compared to 18.5 billion crowns a year earlier.
The 1996 surplus is made up of 9.4 billion crowns in interest received, 200 million in interest expenditure and 4.9 billion crowns in exchange rate effects.

"The smaller surplus on foreign operations in 1996 compared with 1995 is partly a consequence of a lower level of foreign exchange reserves in 1996, but it mainly reflects the greater stability of international interest rates compared with 1995," the bank said in a statement.
"In that the holding of securities is booked at market values, in 1995 the sharp fall in interest rates had a positive effect on the year's results."
The Riksbank said the weaker crown exchange rate towards the end of 1996 combined with the negative forward position at year-end generated a positive valuation effect of 4.9 billion crowns.
The average level of foreign exchange reserves in 1996 was 153.4 billion crowns accompanied by a negative forward exchange position equivalent to 70.1 billion crowns.

Domestic operations in 1996 resulted in a surplus of 4.8 billion crowns compared to 700 million a year earlier. "The improvement came in part from decreased interest expenditure on account of lower interest rates but above all, from a reduced stock of Riksbank liquidity bills," the bank said.

The balance sheet total at the end of 1996 was 212.6 billion crowns against 257.3 billion crowns. The largest asset items are the foreign exchange reserves and the holdings of Swedish government securities.

The book value on the foreign exchange reserves decreased to 140.2 billion crowns from 171.3 billion while the book value of Swedish government securities fell to 59 billion from 71 billion crowns at the end of 1996.
-- Belinda Goldsmith, Stockholm newsroom +46-8-700 1045 ($ = 7.399 Swedish Crowns)
